One Token Away from Collapse:
The Fragility of Instruction-Tuned Helpfulness

Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo* Affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, USA    Seyedarmin Azizi* Affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, USA    Souvik Kundu Affiliation: Intel AI, USA* Equal contribution authors{baghaeip, seyedarm, pedram}@usc.edu, souvikk.kundu@intel.com    Massoud Pedram Affiliation: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, USA
Abstract

Instruction-tuned large language models produce helpful, structured responses, but how robust is this helpfulness when trivially constrained? We show that simple lexical constraints (banning a single punctuation character or common word) cause instruction-tuned LLMs to collapse their responses, losing 14–48% of comprehensiveness in pairwise evaluation across three open-weight model families and one closed-weight model (GPT-4o-mini). The baseline response is preferred in 77–100% of 1,920 pairwise comparisons judged by GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o. Notably, GPT-4o-mini suffers 31% comprehensiveness loss (99% baseline win rate), demonstrating that the fragility extends to commercially deployed closed-weight models, contrary to prior findings on format-level constraints. Through mechanistic analysis, we identify this as a planning failure: two-pass generation (free generation followed by constrained rewriting) recovers 59–96% of response length, and linear probes on prompt representations predict response length with R2=0.51R^{2}=0.51–0.930.93 before generation begins, with R2R^{2} tracking collapse severity across models. The same probes yield negative R2R^{2} on base models, confirming that instruction tuning creates the representational structure encoding the collapse decision. Crucially, base models show no systematic collapse under identical constraints, with effects that are small, noisy, and bidirectional, demonstrating that instruction tuning creates this fragility by coupling task competence to narrow surface-form templates. The effect replicates on MT-Bench across all eight task categories. We further show that standard independent LLM-as-judge evaluation detects only a 3.5% average quality drop where pairwise evaluation reveals 23%, exposing a methodological blind spot in how constrained generation is assessed.

1 Introduction

Instruction tuning, the process of fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on instruction–response pairs, often followed by preference optimization, is the standard recipe for producing helpful AI assistants (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023). The implicit assumption is that instruction tuning teaches generalizable helpfulness: the ability to provide thorough, accurate, and comprehensive responses regardless of surface-level formatting or stylistic choices. A well-aligned model should be able to explain gradient descent equally well whether or not it uses bullet points, commas, or any particular token.

We challenge this assumption. We show that trivially constraining an instruction-tuned model’s surface form (Figure 1: for instance, adding “Do not use any commas in your response” to a question) causes the model to collapse its response. The model does not simply rephrase the same content without commas; it mode-switches to a drastically shorter, less comprehensive response. For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, banning commas reduces response length by 57% and comprehensiveness by 27% in pairwise evaluation. For Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, the same constraint reduces comprehensiveness by 61%. The output remains free-form natural language. This is not a structured output problem. The model simply produces less.

This effect, which we term constraint-induced response collapse, is not a capability limitation. When we let the model generate freely and then rewrite its response under the constraint (a two-pass approach), it retains 59–96% of the original length. The model can write comprehensive comma-free prose; it just does not plan to when the constraint is presented alongside the question. Linear probes on the model’s prompt representations reveal that response length is predictable with R2=0.51R^{2}=0.51–0.930.93 from hidden states at middle layers, before a single token is generated, with R2R^{2} tracking collapse severity across three model families. The same probes applied to base (non-instruction-tuned) models yield negative R2R^{2} at every layer, confirming that instruction tuning creates both the behavioral collapse and the representational structure that encodes it.

The critical evidence comes from comparing instruction-tuned models with their base (non-instruction-tuned) counterparts. Under identical constraints, base models show small, inconsistent effects (baseline win rates of 45–59%, near or at chance), with some constraints actually improving output quality. Instruction tuning transforms this noisy landscape into systematic, severe collapse (77–100% baseline win rates). The fragility is not inherent to language models or to the constraints themselves; it is a specific artifact of instruction tuning, which couples task competence to narrow surface-form templates. Importantly, this fragility extends to closed-weight, commercially deployed models: GPT-4o-mini suffers 31% comprehensiveness loss with a 99% baseline win rate, more than Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (26%), despite substantially more extensive post-training.

We additionally uncover a methodological blind spot: standard independent LLM-as-judge scoring (Zheng et al., 2023), the dominant evaluation paradigm, detects only a 3.5% average quality drop from constraints that cause 23% degradation in pairwise comparison on the same model with the same judge, a 6.7×6.7\times gap. This suggests that the evaluation community may be systematically underestimating quality loss in constrained generation settings.

Contributions.

Our findings contribute to understanding the nature and limitations of post-training alignment:

  1. 1.

    We document constraint-induced response collapse: trivial lexical constraints cause 14–48% comprehensiveness loss across three open-weight instruction-tuned model families and one closed-weight model (GPT-4o-mini), validated by 1,920 pairwise comparisons with two judges (§4).

  2. 2.

    We identify the mechanism as a planning failure, not a capability limitation, through two-pass recovery experiments (59–96% recovery), representation probing (R2=0.51R^{2}=0.51–0.930.93 tracking collapse severity), and base-model control experiments (negative R2R^{2}), replicated across three model families (§5).

  3. 3.

    We show that instruction tuning specifically creates this systematic fragility, while base models across all three families show only small, inconsistent effects (§6).

  4. 4.

    We demonstrate that independent LLM-as-judge evaluation is blind to response collapse, detecting less than one-fifth of the pairwise-measured quality loss (§7).

2 Related Work

Structured output and the format tax.

Tam et al. (2024) first documented that restricting LLMs to structured formats (JSON, XML, YAML) degrades reasoning accuracy by 10–15%. Concurrent work by Lee et al. (2026) systematically measures this “format tax” across ten models and four formats, decomposing degradation into prompt-level (dominant) and decoder-level (minor) components, and finding that closed-weight models largely resist the format tax. Our work differs in three key ways: (i) our constraints are lexical (token bans), not structural (format changes), and the output remains free-form natural language; (ii) our effect sizes are substantially larger (14–48% vs. 5–15%); and (iii) we find that closed-weight models are not protected against lexical constraint collapse: GPT-4o-mini shows 31% comprehensiveness loss, suggesting that the robustness closed-weight models exhibit against format constraints does not transfer to lexical constraints. We additionally provide mechanistic analysis (planning failure, representational encoding) and base-vs-instruct comparison that prior work does not. Deng et al. (2025) propose decoupled generation to separate formatting from reasoning; their approach is complementary to our analysis.

Instruction following and constraint satisfaction.

A growing body of work evaluates whether LLMs satisfy explicit constraints: IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023) introduced verifiable instruction-following benchmarks, and subsequent work has expanded to multi-constraint (He et al., 2024a; Wen et al., 2024), multi-turn (He et al., 2024b), and agentic (Qi et al., 2025) settings. These benchmarks measure constraint satisfaction rates, i.e., whether the model follows the constraint, but do not assess what happens to response quality when constraints are followed. Our work is orthogonal; we show that even when models successfully satisfy a constraint (e.g., 99% comma avoidance), the quality of the satisfying response collapses. Training methods that improve constraint satisfaction (Dong et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025) address a complementary problem.

Constrained decoding.

Grammar-constrained decoding (GCD) (Willard and Louf, 2023; Geng et al., 2023) masks invalid tokens to guarantee structural compliance, while grammar-aligned decoding (Park et al., 2024) corrects the distribution distortion GCD introduces. These operate at the decoder level with formal grammars. Our constraints operate at the prompt level: we do not mask tokens; we ask the model to avoid them via natural language instruction. Lee et al. (2026) show that prompt-level effects dominate decoder-level effects for structured output; we extend this finding to show that prompt-level lexical constraints produce even larger degradation.

Activation steering for instruction following.

Stolfo et al. (2025) use representation engineering to improve instruction-following accuracy via steering vectors. Their work focuses on increasing constraint satisfaction rates (from ∼10%{\sim}10\% to ∼30%{\sim}30\% without explicit text instructions) and does not study quality degradation. Our findings are complementary: understanding the representational basis of collapse could inform better steering interventions.

Robustness and prompt sensitivity.

Prior work has studied LLM sensitivity to prompt phrasing (Sclar et al., 2024; Mizrahi et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2025b), showing that semantically equivalent reformulations can change model behavior. Our setting is distinct: constraints are not paraphrases of the same instruction but rather explicit additions that change the task. The model correctly interprets the constraint; it simply cannot maintain quality while following it.

3 Experimental Setup

Prompts.

We construct a diverse evaluation set of 40 prompts spanning four categories: explanation/education (e.g., “Explain gradient descent in simple terms”), how-to/advice (e.g., “How do I write an effective research paper?”), analysis/comparison (e.g., “Compare renewable and non-renewable energy sources”), and technical/detailed (e.g., “Explain how transformer models process natural language”), with 10 prompts per category.

Constraints.

We define eight lexical constraints organized into three types:

  • •

    Punctuation-level: Ban commas, colons, or semicolons (e.g., “Do not use any commas in your response”).

  • •

    Pattern-level: Ban bullet points, numbered lists, and dashes (“Write only in flowing prose paragraphs”).

  • •

    Word-level: Ban the word “the” or ban discourse markers (“however,” “therefore,” “moreover,” “furthermore,” “additionally”).

We additionally test two compositional constraints: commas+colons and commas+bullets. Each constraint is appended to the prompt as a natural-language instruction. Crucially, the output format remains free-form natural language; no structured output (JSON, XML) is requested.

Models.

We evaluate seven models spanning open-weight, closed-weight, base, and instruction-tuned categories. Open-weight instruction-tuned: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024), and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023). Open-weight base: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B. Closed-weight instruction-tuned: GPT-4o-mini (Hurst et al., 2024), accessed via API. Open-weight models are run locally with bfloat16 precision.

Generation.

For each prompt–constraint pair, we generate three independent samples (temperature 0.7, top-pp 0.9, max 1024 tokens) using the model’s chat template for instruct models and a simple “Question: … Answer:” format for base models. For 40 prompts ×\times 9 conditions (8 constraints + unconstrained baseline) ×\times 3 samples, this yields 1,080 responses per model.

Evaluation.

We employ two evaluation protocols:

  • •

    Independent scoring: A judge model rates each response in isolation on four dimensions (informativeness, depth, clarity, helpfulness) on a 1–10 scale. This mirrors standard practice (Zheng et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023).

  • •

    Pairwise comparison: A judge model sees both the baseline (unconstrained) and constrained responses for the same prompt side-by-side, with positions randomized, and rates each on comprehensiveness and usefulness (1–10). This forces calibration against the full response.

We use GPT-4o-mini as the primary judge (all models) and GPT-4o as a secondary judge (all three open-weight instruct models) to verify judge independence. We report comprehensiveness change (%) relative to the baseline and baseline win rate (fraction of pairs where the baseline is rated more comprehensive).

Constraint satisfaction.

We verify that models actually follow constraints using automated checkers (character/word counters, regex pattern matching). Satisfaction rates are high: 92–100% for most constraints on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (66% for colon avoidance, which interacts with the model’s header-generation behavior; see Appendix F). Since most constraints are satisfied at >>90% rates, the quality collapse we measure is predominantly driven by responses that successfully follow the constraint, not by constraint violations.

4 Constraint-Induced Response Collapse

4.1 Main Results: Pairwise Comparison

Figure 2 presents the central finding: instruction-tuned models systematically lose comprehensiveness under lexical constraints. The effect is consistent across all three open-weight model families, all eight constraint types, and all four prompt categories. Section 4.4 extends this finding to a closed-weight model.

Several patterns emerge. First, the effect is large and consistent: all three instruct models show substantial comprehensiveness loss (14–40% overall), with the unconstrained baseline winning 77–98% of pairwise comparisons. Second, models differ in fragility: Qwen is most fragile (−-39.9%), followed by Llama (−-23.4%) and Mistral (−-14.2%), suggesting that collapse severity varies with instruction-tuning recipe. Third, the effect is not specific to formatting tokens: banning the word “the” (−-22.6% on Llama, −-42.1% on Qwen, −-18.8% on Mistral) causes comparable damage to banning commas (−-27.0%, −-60.9%, −-19.0%), even though “the” plays no formatting role. This indicates the fragility is tied to token frequency and template disruption, not to formatting specifically.

Compositional constraints show a collapse floor.

Banning commas and colons together (−-29.8% on Llama) produces only marginally worse results than banning commas alone (−-27.0%). Once the model enters its minimal response mode, additional constraints have diminishing impact. This suggests a discrete strategy switch rather than continuous degradation.

Underlying response changes.

The comprehensiveness loss reflects dramatic structural changes. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, banning commas reduces average response length by 57% (from 685 to 297 tokens), unique content words by 41%, and formatting richness (presence of bold text, headers, code blocks, bullet points) from 2.3 to 0.4 on a 0–4 scale. The model does not simply write the same content without commas; it produces a fundamentally different, minimal response.

4.2 Cross-Judge Validation

To verify that our findings are not judge-dependent, we repeat the pairwise evaluation with GPT-4o as judge for all three instruct models (Table 1).

The stronger judge consistently detects larger degradation across all three models (−-17.4% vs. −-14.2% for Mistral; −-25.9% vs. −-23.4% for Llama; −-48.1% vs. −-39.9% for Qwen), while baseline win rates remain stable. This confirms that the effect is judge-independent and that more discriminating judges reveal more severe collapse.

4.3 Category Consistency

The collapse holds across all four prompt categories (Table 2), ruling out domain-specific explanations. Technical prompts show the largest decline on Llama (−-26.7%), consistent with the expectation that structured, detail-rich content depends most on the formatting patterns disrupted by lexical constraints.

4.4 Extension to a Closed-Weight Model

A natural question is whether the collapse is specific to open-weight 7–8B models or extends to commercially deployed systems with more extensive post-training. To test this, we evaluate GPT-4o-mini (Hurst et al., 2024) under identical constraints, generating one response per prompt–constraint pair via the OpenAI API (temperature 0.7, max 1024 tokens) and judging with GPT-4o.

GPT-4o-mini shows severe collapse (Table 3): −-31% overall comprehensiveness loss with a 99.1% baseline win rate across 320 pairwise comparisons. Banning commas causes −-42% degradation, and average response length drops from 472 to 216 words (−-54%). The per-constraint pattern mirrors the open-weight models: comma bans are most damaging, bullet point bans least, and word-level constraints (“the,” discourse markers) produce intermediate degradation.

Contrast with prior work.

This result stands in contrast to Lee et al. (2026), who found that closed-weight models largely resist the format tax on structured output. The distinction is instructive: format-level constraints (“output as JSON”) may have been addressed through targeted structured-output fine-tuning, while lexical constraints (“do not use commas”) represent a class of restrictions that even extensive post-training does not anticipate. The robustness that closed-weight models have developed against format constraints does not transfer to lexical constraints; these are distinct failure modes requiring distinct solutions.

4.5 Validation on MT-Bench

To verify that our findings generalize beyond our evaluation prompts, we replicate the experiment on MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023), a standard 80-question benchmark spanning eight categories: writing, roleplay, reasoning, math, coding, extraction, STEM, and humanities. We test Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct under three constraints (no comma, no “the,” no bullet), with GPT-4o as judge (240 pairwise comparisons per model).

The results closely replicate our main findings (Figure 3). Qwen shows −-40.5% overall comprehensiveness loss (89% baseline win rate) on MT-Bench, nearly identical to the −-39.9% on our evaluation set. Llama shows −-17.2% (74% win rate), consistent with its −-23.4% on our prompts. Per-constraint patterns are preserved: comma bans are most damaging (Llama −-26%, Qwen −-65%), followed by “the” (Llama −-19%, Qwen −-42%) and bullet bans (Llama −-5%, Qwen −-12%).

The category breakdown reveals that the collapse spans all task types, including those not represented in our evaluation set. STEM (−-25% to −-46%), reasoning (−-20% to −-50%), and coding (−-16% to −-48%) all show substantial degradation. The one exception is Llama on math (+3%, chance-level win rate): its math responses are short and formulaic, not relying on the structured templates that collapse under constraints. Qwen, more aggressively template-dependent, collapses even on math (−-51%). This exception is itself informative: tasks whose optimal responses do not depend on structured formatting templates are naturally less vulnerable, confirming the template-dependence mechanism.

5 Mechanistic Analysis: Why Does Collapse Happen?

The previous section establishes that constraint-induced collapse occurs. We now investigate why, through a series of experiments that progressively localize the mechanism. All experiments are replicated across three instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B).

5.1 It Is a Planning Failure, Not a Capability Limitation

Motivation.

The collapse could reflect either (a) the model genuinely cannot express complex content under constraints, or (b) the model’s planning mechanism selects a minimal response strategy when it encounters a constraint, despite having the capability to produce comprehensive constrained output. We distinguish these hypotheses using a two-pass protocol.

Method.

For each of 10 prompts and 2 constraints (no comma, no “the”), we generate: (1) a baseline response (no constraint), (2) a single-pass response (constraint in prompt), and (3) a two-pass response (generate baseline, then rewrite it under the constraint with explicit instruction to maintain comprehensiveness). We measure word-level length retention relative to the baseline.

Results (Table 4).

All three models confirm the planning failure hypothesis. On Llama and Mistral, single-pass retains 49–52% of baseline length, while two-pass retains 91–96%, achieving near-perfect recovery. Llama’s no-comma constraint achieves 100% retention in two-pass: the model produces responses of virtually identical length to the unconstrained baseline.

Qwen tells a more nuanced story. Two-pass recovers substantially for “no the” (16%→\to79%) but only partially for “no comma” (9%→\to40%). Inspection reveals that some Qwen comma-free rewrites collapse to 0–4 words. For Qwen, commas appear so deeply embedded in generation patterns that even explicit rewriting fails for certain content types. The mechanism is thus primarily a planning failure, with a secondary capability limitation for high-frequency syntactic tokens in more aggressively tuned models.

5.2 Collapse Is Pre-Determined in Prompt Representations

Motivation.

If the collapse is a planning failure, the decision should be detectable in the model’s representations before generation begins.

Method.

For each of 40 prompts ×\times 3 conditions (baseline, no comma, no “the”) = 120 prompt variants, we extract hidden states at the last prompt token across five evenly-spaced layers. We train Ridge regression probes via 5-fold cross-validation to predict response length (token count, averaged over 3 samples) from these representations. Response lengths are pre-computed from our generation results.

Note on constraint classification. Since constrained prompts contain additional text (the constraint instruction), a classifier can trivially distinguish them. We therefore focus on length prediction R2R^{2} as the scientifically meaningful test: can the model’s representations predict how much it will generate, not just whether a constraint is present?

Results (Table 5).

A simple linear probe explains 51–93% of the variance in response length from the last prompt token’s hidden state at the middle layer. All three models show a consistent layer profile: R2R^{2} jumps sharply in early layers, peaks at ∼{\sim}50% depth, and plateaus or slightly decreases toward the final layer. This suggests that early-to-middle layers translate constraint detection into a response strategy, which is then maintained through the rest of the network.

R2R^{2} tracks collapse severity.

A striking pattern emerges across models: probing R2R^{2} correlates with behavioral collapse severity (Table 6). Qwen, the most fragile model (−-48%), yields R2=0.93R^{2}=0.93; Llama (−-26%) yields R2=0.75R^{2}=0.75; and Mistral, the most robust (−-17%), yields R2=0.51R^{2}=0.51. The more deterministic the collapse, the more predictable it is from representations. This is consistent with a shared mechanism operating at different intensities: more aggressively instruction-tuned models encode a more deterministic collapse plan in their middle-layer representations.

Control experiment: base models do not encode collapse.

To verify that the probing result reflects instruction-tuning-specific representational structure rather than a general property of language models, we repeat the experiment on the corresponding base models (Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B) under identical conditions.

The contrast is stark (Table 7). Base models yield negative R2R^{2} at every probed layer (Llama: −-4.04; Qwen: −-0.59), meaning the probe performs worse than predicting the mean. Response length is entirely unpredictable from base model representations. Qwen base’s average lengths (156 vs. 153 words for unconstrained vs. constrained) confirm there is virtually no length difference to predict.

This result connects the behavioral and representational levels of analysis: instruction tuning simultaneously creates (1) the template-dependent response strategy that collapses under constraints, and (2) the representational encoding of that strategy in middle-layer hidden states. Base models possess neither. We further validate the behavioral side of this claim in §6, where pairwise evaluation confirms that base models show no systematic collapse.

5.3 Strategy Divergence Is Immediate

Method.

We run the model forward token-by-token on 5 prompts ×\times 2 constraints, recording the top-50 token probability distribution at each of the first 20 generated positions for both the constrained and unconstrained prompts. We measure Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) and top-50 token overlap at each position.

Results (Table 8).

All three models show the same pattern: distributions diverge substantially within positions 1–3 (JSD = 0.46–0.54) and are nearly fully separated by position 5–10 (JSD >> 0.8). Qualitatively, unconstrained Llama opens with markdown formatting (e.g., “**Gradient Descent: A Simple Explanation**”) while the constrained model opens with plain prose (“Gradient descent is a way to find”), committing to a fundamentally different response strategy in the very first token.

6 Instruction Tuning Systematizes Fragility

The analysis above characterizes collapse in instruction-tuned models. A natural question is whether this fragility is inherent to language models or specific to instruction tuning. We answer this by running the identical experiment on non-instruction-tuned (base) counterparts for all three model families.

Figure 4 reveals a striking contrast across all model types. Base models exhibit small, noisy effects: Qwen base shows ++7.1% improvement (the constrained response wins more often), Llama base shows −-7.5% with a 55% win rate (near chance), and Mistral base shows −-11.2% with a 59% win rate. In contrast, all four instruction-tuned models show severe, systematic collapse, ranging from Mistral instruct at −-17.4% (78% win rate) to Qwen instruct at −-48.1% (99.7%). GPT-4o-mini, the only closed-weight model, falls squarely in the middle of the instruct models at −-31.0% (99.1%), confirming that the fragility is a property of instruction tuning broadly, not a quirk of small open-weight models.

The within-family comparisons are particularly informative. The same Qwen-2.5-7B architecture goes from constraints improving output (++7.1%) to catastrophic collapse (−-48.1%), a 55-percentage-point swing in win rate caused entirely by post-training alignment. Llama shows a 42-percentage-point swing (55%→\to97.5%) and even Mistral, the most robust instruct model, shows a 19-point swing (59%→\to78%).

Why constraints sometimes help base models.

Base model output is often unstructured and repetitive. Constraints like “no bullet points” or “no commas” can force the base model into more focused, coherent prose, inadvertently improving quality. The instruction-tuned model, whose unconstrained output is already its best-learned strategy, has no room for such accidental improvement.

Interpretation.

Instruction tuning does not create constraint sensitivity ex nihilo; all three base models show some degradation for individual constraints (e.g., Mistral base reaches −-11.2% overall, with certain constraints producing larger effects). What instruction tuning does is transform this noisy, inconsistent landscape into systematic, unidirectional collapse. The mechanism is template dependence: instruction tuning teaches the model a narrow repertoire of high-quality response templates (structured, formatted, comprehensive). When constraints block the key tokens these templates depend on, the model lacks an alternative comprehensive strategy and falls back to a minimal response mode. Base models, lacking such templates, have less to collapse from.

7 The Blindness of Independent Evaluation

Our pairwise evaluation protocol was motivated by an observation in our initial experiments: standard independent scoring dramatically underestimates the quality impact of lexical constraints.

Table 9 shows the discrepancy: independent scoring detects an average 3.5% quality drop, while pairwise comparison reveals 23.4%, a 6.7×6.7\times difference. For the no-bullet constraint, independent scoring detects zero degradation despite a 12.9% pairwise-measured drop.

Why does this happen?

In independent evaluation, the judge assesses each response in isolation against an implicit quality standard. Constrained responses, while shorter and less comprehensive, are often locally coherent: each sentence is accurate and well-formed. Without seeing the full baseline response, the judge lacks a calibration reference and assigns inflated scores. The baseline composite score (8.54/10) and the constrained composite (7.94–8.54/10) both fall in the “good to very good” range, masking the large gap in actual comprehensiveness.

Implications.

This finding has consequences beyond our specific study. Any evaluation of constrained generation systems, including structured output, style-controlled generation, safety-filtered generation, or length-controlled generation, that relies solely on independent scoring may systematically underestimate quality loss. We recommend pairwise evaluation as the default for settings where constraints may reduce response comprehensiveness.

8 Discussion

What instruction tuning actually learns.

Our results suggest that instruction tuning’s apparent helpfulness is, at least in part, an artifact of learning a narrow distribution of response templates rather than developing a generalizable competence for providing thorough and accurate information. When any high-frequency token is banned, whether a formatting character (comma), a structural element (bullet points), or a common content word (“the”), the model’s learned templates become inaccessible, and it defaults to a minimal response. The two-pass recovery result confirms this interpretation: the underlying knowledge and capability are intact, but the model’s generation planning mechanism cannot access them when the constraint is presented upfront. The base model probing control (§5.2) provides the representational counterpart to this behavioral finding: instruction tuning creates not only the template-dependent strategy but also the internal structure that encodes the collapse decision, which is entirely absent in base models.

Lexical constraints as diagnostic probes.

A natural objection is that the specific constraints we study are artificial: no real user asks “explain gradient descent without commas.” This is by design. Our lexical constraints serve as controlled diagnostic probes, analogous to stress tests in structural engineering: no one drives a 100-ton truck across a pedestrian bridge in normal use, but if the bridge collapses under that load, it reveals something important about the bridge’s structural integrity that normal foot traffic would never expose. The value of our constraints lies not in their realism, but in what they reveal: instruction-tuned helpfulness is contingent on the model’s ability to use its preferred surface-form patterns.

This finding has direct practical relevance. In real-world deployments, models routinely operate under constraints that restrict their surface form, not as “ban commas,” but in functionally analogous ways. Safety filters prohibit specific tokens or phrases. Brand guidelines restrict tone, formatting, or punctuation (e.g., “no exclamation marks, no casual language”). Accessibility requirements mandate simplified sentence structures. Legal compliance rules forbid definitive claims. Content policies ban certain terminology. Localization guidelines restrict idioms and region-specific references. Any of these may disrupt the same formatting templates our lexical constraints disrupt, potentially triggering analogous collapse. Our finding that even the simplest possible constraint (banning a single punctuation character) causes 14–48% comprehensiveness loss suggests that this class of fragility is pervasive and warrants systematic investigation in deployed systems.

Implications for evaluation and deployment.

The 6.7×6.7\times gap between independent and pairwise evaluation (§7) implies that any constrained generation system evaluated solely by independent scoring may carry undetected quality loss. For deployment, the GPT-4o-mini result (§4.4) makes the concern concrete: a widely deployed commercial model loses 31% of comprehensiveness under a trivial constraint. Practitioners should test their deployed models against the specific constraints they impose, using pairwise evaluation.

Toward robust instruction tuning.

Our analysis suggests that constraint robustness should become an explicit training objective. The two-pass recovery result demonstrates feasibility: models possess the capability to produce comprehensive constrained output. The probing results localize the planning failure to middle-layer representations (∼{\sim}50% depth across all three architectures), identifying a consistent intervention site. The finding that R2R^{2} tracks collapse severity (Table 6) suggests that reducing representational determinism at these layers may mitigate the collapse. Promising directions include constraint-augmented alignment training (Yuan et al., 2024), representation-level interventions (Stolfo et al., 2025), and training with diverse surface-form constraints to decouple competence from any particular template.

Limitations.

Our mechanistic analysis is conducted on three 7–8B parameter open-weight models; we cannot determine whether the internal mechanism is identical in closed-weight models like GPT-4o-mini, though the behavioral signature is the same. Our pairwise evaluation uses LLM judges, which may have their own biases; the use of GPT-4o to judge GPT-4o-mini introduces a same-family concern, though our cross-judge validation (§4.2) supports GPT-4o’s reliability as a discriminating judge. Our constraint set, while diverse, does not exhaustively cover all possible lexical constraints. The base model probing control uses 30 samples (vs. 120 for instruct), though the negative R2R^{2} at all layers is unambiguous regardless of sample size. The mechanistic analysis uses linear probes, which may underestimate the complexity of the underlying representation.

9 Conclusion

We have shown that instruction-tuned LLMs suffer from constraint-induced response collapse: trivial lexical constraints cause 14–48% comprehensiveness loss across four instruction-tuned models, including the closed-weight GPT-4o-mini (−-31%), with the unconstrained baseline preferred in 77–100% of pairwise comparisons. This collapse is a planning failure, not a capability limitation: two-pass recovery reaches 59–96%, and the collapse is pre-determined in middle-layer prompt representations (R2=0.51R^{2}=0.51–0.930.93), with R2R^{2} tracking collapse severity across three model families. Critically, base models exhibit neither systematic behavioral collapse nor the representational structure that encodes it (negative R2R^{2} at all layers), demonstrating that instruction tuning creates both the fragility and its internal encoding. The finding that closed-weight models are not immune (contrary to observations on format-level constraints) suggests that lexical constraint collapse is a fundamental property of the instruction-tuning paradigm. Our finding that standard independent evaluation is blind to this collapse (detecting <<20% of the true effect) carries methodological implications for how constrained generation systems are assessed. We hope this work contributes to developing more robust alignment procedures that teach generalizable helpfulness rather than template-dependent fluency.

Appendix E Two-Pass Qualitative Examples

We present a representative example from the two-pass experiment (§5.1) on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct: the prompt “Explain how vaccines work to protect against diseases” under the constraint “Do not use the word ‘the’ in your response.”

Analysis. The single-pass response collapses to a single paragraph of 55 words, losing all structure, examples, and step-by-step detail, while the two-pass response preserves the original’s numbered structure, bold headers, and substantive content while successfully avoiding the word “the.” This demonstrates that the model can produce comprehensive constraint-satisfying output; it simply fails to do so when the constraint is presented alongside the question.

Appendix F Constraint Satisfaction Rates

Table 14 reports constraint satisfaction rates for each model–constraint pair. Satisfaction is measured by automated checkers (character/word counters, regex pattern matching). Rates are generally high (>>90%), confirming that the quality collapse we report occurs among responses that successfully follow the constraint, not among responses that fail to follow it.

Note on colon satisfaction for Llama.

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct achieves only 65.8% satisfaction for the no-colon constraint because the model frequently generates headers with colons (e.g., “Step 1: ...”) as part of its learned formatting templates. This is itself evidence of template dependence: the model struggles to suppress even a single punctuation character when it conflicts with deeply ingrained formatting patterns. Since pairwise evaluation includes all responses regardless of satisfaction status, the reported comprehensiveness drop for this constraint is conservative: non-satisfying responses (which retain more baseline-like formatting) attenuate the measured effect.
